subtitleHtml: Introduction to Robotics (700.820), Lecture 3 — Narendiran Anandan, Serkan Ergun. Slides from winter term 2025 (25W).

headings.text: Recap: robot control system and components

html:
The big picture

Sensors bring the world into the computer; actuators carry the computer's decisions back out, turning energy and control signals into motion. They are grouped by the energy they use. Fluid actuators push with pressure: hydraulic ones (liquid, 100–300 bar) give the largest forces, pneumatic ones (air, 5–7 bar) are cleaner and simpler but weaker, and vacuum grippers pull by sucking. Smaller niches are filled by piezoelectric, magnetic, thermal and shape-memory actuators. Robots mostly use electric motors: a plain DC motor spins, a servo adds a position sensor and closed-loop control, a stepper moves in fixed steps without feedback. The second half is a toolbox of mechanical engineering quantities that describe what an actuator delivers: force, pressure (F = pA), stress, torque (M = r \times F), work/energy, power (P = Fv = M\omega = UI) and efficiency (\eta = P_{out}/P_{in}), which multiplies along a drive chain.

Recap: robot control system and components

Sensors → ADC → Computer → DAC / drivers → Actuators

The slide shows a mobile manipulator: sensor signals are digitised (ADC) for the computer, and the computer's commands are converted back (DAC) and amplified by drivers to move the actuators.

Recap: sensors and actuators

  • Sensors are devices that produce an output signal in response to some physical parameter in the environment.
  • An actuator is a device that produces a motion by converting energy and signals going into the system.

Actuator types

  • Hydraulic actuators (fluids)
  • Pneumatic actuators (gases, e.g. air or N₂) / vacuum
  • Mechanical actuators (e.g. manual)
  • Piezoelectric actuators (deformation through electric input)
  • Magnetic actuators
  • Thermal actuators & (magnetic) memory alloys

  • Electrical motors:

    • Alternating current (AC) motors
    • Direct current (DC) motors
    • Servo motors
    • Stepper motors
  • Combinations (electro-mechanical, electro-hydraulic)

There are also other types of actuators.

Actuators on a wheeled robot

Two tasks: movement & gripping.

A mobile manipulator: an arm with rotary motors in its joints, a linear motor in the gripper, and 4× wheel motors in the base.

  • How many actuators does this wheeled robot have?
  • Why do most serial robots have 6 joints (= motors)?
What are the answers? (try first)
  • Counting: the arm's joints each have a rotary motor (a typical arm like the one pictured has 6), the gripper has a linear motor, and the base has 4 wheel motors — about 11 actuators in total. Movement (wheels) and gripping (arm + gripper) are separate tasks with separate actuators.
  • Why 6 joints: a rigid object in 3D space has 6 degrees of freedom — 3 for position and 3 for orientation (1 Introduction). Each joint adds one DoF, so 6 joints are the minimum to put the end effector at any reachable position with any orientation. Fewer joints restrict the reachable poses; more joints are possible (redundancy) but cost money and complicate control.

Hydraulic actuators

  • Uses pressurised liquids to drive actuators (100–300 bar).
  • High power output; liquid "easy" to transport.
  • Can hold force without consuming additional fluid, due to the incompressibility of fluids.
  • Fluid leakage (contamination).
  • Needs regular maintenance and cleaning.
  • Needs many complementary parts (reservoir, compressor, pump, valves, releases, heat exchangers).

A hydraulic circuit: pump and filter draw from the reservoir, a control valve directs the pressurised fluid to one side of the cylinder, and the return flow goes back to the reservoir.

Force: for a hydraulic cylinder,

p = \frac{F}{A}, \qquad F = pA, \qquad A_{left} \ne A_{right}, \qquad A_{right} = \frac{(D^2 - d^2)\pi}{4}
Symbols
  • p — hydraulic pressure of the oil (Pa = N/m²; often given in bar, 1\,\mathrm{bar} = 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa})
  • F — force the piston delivers (N)
  • A — the piston area the pressure acts on (m²)
  • A_{left} — full piston area (the side without the rod); A_{right} — the ring-shaped area on the rod side, smaller because the rod covers part of the piston
  • D — piston (cylinder bore) diameter (m); d — piston rod diameter (m)

Power:

P = pQ

where Q is the flow rate, [Q] = \mathrm{m^3/s}.

Symbols
  • P — hydraulic power (W)
  • p — pressure (Pa)
  • Q — volume flow rate of the oil (m³/s) — here not heat or charge

The slide also shows a hydraulic rotational motor. There are also many other types…

Why are the two sides of a cylinder different, A_{left} \ne A_{right}?

The piston rod is attached to one side only. Pressure on the side without the rod acts on the full circle, \frac{\pi D^2}{4} (piston diameter D). On the rod side, the rod takes up part of the area, leaving a ring, \frac{(D^2 - d^2)\pi}{4} (rod diameter d). Same pressure, smaller area → the cylinder pulls back with less force than it pushes out.

Why is hydraulic power P = pQ?

Pressure is force per area, and flow rate is volume per time: p \cdot Q = \frac{F}{A} \cdot \frac{A\,s}{t} = F \cdot \frac{s}{t} = F v — force times velocity, which is mechanical power. Units check: \mathrm{Pa} \cdot \mathrm{m^3/s} = \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m^2}} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{m^3}}{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{\mathrm{N\,m}}{\mathrm{s}} = \mathrm{W}.

Worked example: sizing a hydraulic cylinder

Piston diameter D = 50\,\mathrm{mm}, rod d = 20\,\mathrm{mm}, pressure 150\,\mathrm{bar}, flow 10\,\mathrm{L/min}.

  • Convert to SI: p = 150 \cdot 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} = 1.5 \cdot 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa}; Q = \frac{10 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}}{60\,\mathrm{s}} \approx 1.67 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}.
  • Push (full area): A = \frac{\pi \cdot 0.05^2}{4} \approx 1.96 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}, so F = pA \approx 29.5\,\mathrm{kN} — about the weight of 3 tonnes.
  • Pull (ring area): A = \frac{(0.05^2 - 0.02^2)\pi}{4} \approx 1.65 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}, so F \approx 24.7\,\mathrm{kN}.
  • Hydraulic power: P = pQ = 1.5 \cdot 10^7 \cdot 1.67 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{W} \approx 2.5\,\mathrm{kW}.

Pneumatic actuators

  • Somewhat similar to hydraulic actuators.
  • Uses pressurised gas (air) to drive actuators (typ. 5–7 bar).
  • Much lower pressure (vs. hydraulic) – lower forces – why?
  • Gas (air) leakage (less contamination than hydraulic).
  • Gas is usually condensed with oil for less friction (contamination in clean rooms / food industry).
  • Fewer tubes (vs. hydraulic).
  • Needs regular maintenance and cleaning.
  • Needs complementary parts (pressure tank, compressor, valves, releases).

Force, pressure and power are calculated identically to hydraulic systems.

Pictured: a pneumatic circuit diagram, a pneumatic gripper and an air bellows.

Why do pneumatic systems work at much lower pressure?

Gas is compressible, liquid is not. Compressed air stores a lot of energy, like a compressed spring: if a high-pressure air line bursts, that energy is released violently, while a hydraulic leak just squirts liquid. So air systems are kept at a few bar for safety, and with F = pA, lower pressure means lower force for the same cylinder. The compressibility also makes pneumatic actuators springy: they're great for fast "open/closed" motions like grippers, but poor at holding a precise intermediate position under varying load, where hydraulics' incompressibility wins.

Vacuum actuator

  • "Opposite" of a pneumatic actuator → uses "negative pressure".
  • Uses suction to reduce pressure in an enclosed chamber.
  • Lower forces (compared to pneumatic actuators).
  • System needs to be airtight (no leakage).
  • Needs regular maintenance.
  • Needs complementary parts (pumps, valves, releases).
  • Mainly used for handling low-weight, fragile parts.

Vacuum actuator equations

\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0}, \qquad F = pA
Symbols
  • \sigma — (mechanical) stress: force per area (Pa = N/m²)
  • F — force (N); A_0 — the area the force acts on (m²)
  • p — pressure difference between outside air and the vacuum inside the suction cup (Pa); A — suction area (m²)
  • Force, pressure and power are calculated again in a similar way. The minimum achievable pressure difference is ideally 0 bar (total vacuum). Typically, vacuum actuators operate with 60–80% vacuum (0.2–0.4 bar).
  • At 100% vacuum, theoretically a 1 kg weight can be lifted with a suction area of 1 cm². Forces due to acceleration need to be considered as well (→ PFE* class); for horizontal movement, friction forces apply (again PFE).
  • Due to inaccuracies in surface structure, vacuum stability and workplace safety, a safety factor S of 2 is typically used for suction grippers → only 0.5 kg weight per cm² area for 100% vacuum.
  • Safety factors are quite commonly used in mechanical engineering to conservatively consider (complex) influence factors.

* PFE: Physics for Engineers: Kinematics, Dynamics and Thermodynamics (700.150 + 700.151 to 154).

Why does 1 cm² at full vacuum hold about 1 kg?

A suction cup doesn't "pull": the surrounding air pressure pushes the object against the cup, and full vacuum inside means the whole atmospheric pressure, about 1\,\mathrm{bar} = 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}, is unbalanced. On 1\,\mathrm{cm^2} = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2} that gives F = pA = 10^5 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N} = 10\,\mathrm{N} — the weight of about 1\,\mathrm{kg} (m g \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{N}). That is also why a vacuum gripper can never exceed 1 bar of pressure difference, whatever pump you use.

Worked example: sizing a suction gripper

A robot must lift a 2\,\mathrm{kg} box with a vacuum of 70% (pressure difference 0.7\,\mathrm{bar}) and safety factor S = 2.

  • Force with safety factor: F = S \cdot m g = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 9.81\,\mathrm{N} \approx 39.2\,\mathrm{N}.
  • Pressure in SI: \Delta p = 0.7 \cdot 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}.
  • Required area: A = \frac{F}{\Delta p} = \frac{39.2}{70\,000}\,\mathrm{m^2} \approx 5.6 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2} = 5.6\,\mathrm{cm^2}.

Accelerating the box quickly would add m a to the force — the PFE point on the slide.

Piezoelectric actuator

  • Converts electric energy into mechanical displacement (or stress) → piezoelectric effect.
  • Both "directions" can be used, e.g. use displacement/stress, or use the electric output.
  • Works in piezoelectric materials (most common: quartz, SiO₂).
  • Applications: precise displacement, short electric pulses.

Pictured: a piezo buzzer, a lighter and a fuel injector; and diagrams of piezo materials converting between mechanical and electrical energy (Chen et al., Chemical Science, 2024).

Intuition: one effect, two directions

Squeeze a piezo crystal and it produces a voltage (that's how a lighter's spark or a piezo sensor works). Apply a voltage and it deforms by a tiny amount (that's the actuator). The displacements are only micrometres, but very fast and very precise — ideal for fuel injectors, ultrasound emitters and nanometre positioning stages.

Magnetic actuator

  • Uses magnetic forces to attract and repel (ferromagnetic) objects.
  • Most systems use a combined electro-magnetic approach (coil + core).
  • Force is dependent on the "magnetic cross-section" and number of poles.
  • Pros/cons: does not work with non-(ferro)magnetic objects.
  • Applications: pictured — a scrap-metal crane magnet, a magnetic lifter, and solenoid valves.

Thermal actuator

  • Uses thermal energy to expand volumes or for phase changes (solid to liquid → wax). Usually electrical energy is used.
  • Mainly used for linear actuation or valves.
  • Advantages: compact size, low maintenance, low noise.

Pictured: a wax actuator with its piston retracted in the "cold position" (solid wax) and extended in the "hot position" (liquid wax).

Shape memory actuators

  • When a thermal memory alloy is deformed in its "cold stage", it will "remember" its previous form when heat is applied.
  • For magnetic alloys → when an external magnetic field is applied.
  • Use thermal or magnetic energy to trigger the memory alloy.

Pictured: a magnetic shape-memory (MSM) crystal pushing a piston against a spring when a magnetic field H is applied.

Electric motors

Simple DC motor

A DC motor works on the principle that whenever a current-carrying conductor is placed inside a magnetic field, it experiences a magnetic force whose direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

A coil (armature) between a south and a north pole; the brushes and commutator segments connect it to the battery. The forces F on the two sides of the coil point in opposite directions and turn it.

What is the commutator for?

The force on each side of the coil depends on the current direction. After half a turn, the side that was pushed up is now on the other side and would be pushed back — the coil would just rock and stop. The commutator (a split ring touching the brushes) reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the force always turns it the same way. Brushes rub, so they wear; "brushless" DC motors do the switching electronically instead.

Intuition: Fleming's left-hand rule

Hold your left hand with thumb, index and middle finger at right angles. First finger = Field (N → S), seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force). Point two of them along the known directions and the third shows the remaining one.

AC motors

  • AC motors are electro-mechanical devices powered by alternating current to produce rotational motion.
  • AC motors will be either single- or three-phase.
  • Single-phase motors are not self-starting.
  • Heavier than DC motors, lower torque on startup.
  • Not commonly used in robotics.

Servo motor

  • Motor with position encoder.
  • Position control using closed-loop control.
  • Can rotate the shaft to a specific position.
  • Widely used in robotic joints for precise positioning.
  • Used in camera autofocus.
  • Used in antenna/telescope orientation controls.
  • DC motor.
  • There are also servos with AC motors.

Pictured: the inside of a hobby servo — drive gears, a potentiometer as position sensor, an integrated circuit, and the motor.

Stepper motor

  • A stepper motor rotates with a fixed step angle.
  • Divides a full rotation into a number of steps.
  • Highly accurate positioning can be performed.
  • Can be driven forward or backward.
  • Open-loop control, encoder possible.
  • Lower efficiency.
  • Torque declines rapidly with speed.
  • Application: printers (inkjet, 3D), scanners.

The rotor (a magnet) follows the energised stator poles step by step: 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, 180°.

Intuition: why a stepper needs no feedback

Each electrical pulse switches the stator magnets one position further, and the rotor magnet snaps along by exactly one step angle. With a common step angle of 1.8^\circ, a full turn is \frac{360^\circ}{1.8^\circ} = 200 steps. Counting pulses tells you the angle — no sensor needed (open loop). That only works if the motor never misses a step: overload it or drive it too fast (torque falls with speed) and it silently loses steps, and the controller doesn't notice.

Common mistake: servo vs stepper

Both position precisely, but differently. A servo measures its actual position with an encoder and corrects errors continuously (closed loop); disturb it and it fights back. A stepper is commanded step by step and assumes it got there (open loop). Steppers are simpler and cheaper; servos are reliable under changing loads, which is why robot joints mostly use servos.

Combinations

An electric motor combined with a hydraulic actuator (an electro-hydraulic linear actuator), and an electric motor combined with a cable-driven gripper.

Introduction to mechanical engineering

What is mechanical engineering?

"Mechanical engineering is the study of machines that may involve force and movement." — Wikipedia, November 2023

"Mechanical engineering deals with the design, development and production of machines and systems." — TU Vienna

It deals with physics, statics, dynamics, material science & engineering, thermodynamics, manufacturing, vibration, control theory, …

Don't worry, we'll just cover some basic terms, units & equations.

Force, pressure, stress

  • A force \vec F is an influence that expresses physical impact. Force is a vector (it has a magnitude and a direction): \vec F = \begin{pmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_z \end{pmatrix}, e.g. \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}.
  • Unit: 1 N (newton).
  • Mechanical force: \vec F = p \vec A (from pressure on an area), \vec F(t) = m\,\vec a(t) (if we are on earth and not aboard a rocket); constant acceleration, e.g. gravity close to the earth's surface.
  • Other forces: electrical, magnetic, atomic, …
  • Pressure p is simply the amount of (pressing) force distributed on a surface: F = pA. Unit: 1\,\mathrm{N/m^2} = 1\,\mathrm{Pa}; 1\,\mathrm{bar} = 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}.
  • Pressure is, in general, not equally distributed, but can be assumed equally distributed for some cases. It is a scalar.
  • Stress is a more general term for force per unit surface. It is a tensor (3×3 matrix) consisting of normal and shear stress components:
\begin{pmatrix} \sigma_x & \tau_{xy} & \tau_{xz} \\ \tau_{yx} & \sigma_y & \tau_{yz} \\ \tau_{zx} & \tau_{zy} & \sigma_z \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z — normal stresses: force per area acting perpendicular to a face, pulling or pushing (Pa)
  • \tau_{xy} etc. — shear stresses: force per area acting along a face; first index = the face's normal direction, second index = the force direction (Pa) — here \tau is not torque
Common mistake: bar and pascal

1\,\mathrm{bar} = 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} = 10^5\,\mathrm{N/m^2}. A pascal is tiny (about the pressure of a sheet of paper lying on a table), so engineering pressures are given in bar or MPa. Before using F = pA, convert to Pa and m²: mixing bar with cm² is off by a factor that's easy to get wrong (1\,\mathrm{bar} on 1\,\mathrm{cm^2} is 10\,\mathrm{N}, as in the vacuum example).

Mechanical stress / stress–strain diagram

\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{L - L_0}{L_0}
Symbols
  • \sigma — stress (Pa): force per original cross-section
  • F — the tensile force on the sample (N); A_0 — its original cross-sectional area (m²)
  • \varepsilon — strain (dimensionless, often in %): relative change in length
  • L — current length (m); L_0 — original length (m)

Stress–strain curve of a ductile material (e.g. construction-grade steel): elastic deformation up to the yield strength ("use" region, slope = Young's modulus E), then plastic deformation — strain hardening up to the ultimate strength ("metal forming"), necking, and fracture ("cutting").

E = \text{Young's modulus} = \text{slope} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}
Symbols
  • E — Young's modulus (Pa, usually GPa): stiffness of the material, E = \sigma / \varepsilon in the straight (elastic) part of the curve — "rise" is stress, "run" is strain

The slide also compares brittle and ductile materials: the area under the curve is the energy absorbed before breaking.

Intuition: reading the stress–strain curve

Pull on a steel bar and measure stress (force per original area) against strain (relative stretch). In the straight first part the bar behaves like a spring: let go and it returns to its original length (elastic). Machine parts must stay in this region in use. Beyond the yield strength the deformation becomes permanent (plastic) — useful for forming metal (bending, pressing). The peak is the ultimate strength; after that the bar narrows locally (necking) and finally breaks — which is what cutting exploits.

Torque (moment of force – moment(um))

  • Torque is the "rotational analogue" of a (linear) force.
  • Common symbols: \tau, T, M.
  • Unit: Nm.
  • It is a pseudo-vector given by the cross product of the force and the corresponding lever vector:
\vec M = \vec r \times \vec F
Symbols
  • \vec M — torque (N·m), a vector along the rotation axis
  • \vec r — lever vector: from the rotation axis to the point where the force acts (m)
  • \vec F — the force (N); \times — cross product (magnitude rF\sin\theta, direction by the right-hand rule)
  • Forces → linear motion; torque → rotational motion.

Illustration: a wrench with the force applied at a right angle at distance r.

Worked example: torque on a wrench

A force of 50\,\mathrm{N} is applied at the end of a 0.3\,\mathrm{m} wrench.

  • At a right angle (the best case): M = rF = 0.3 \cdot 50 = 15\,\mathrm{Nm}.
  • At 30^\circ to the handle: only the perpendicular part of the force turns the bolt: M = rF\sin 30^\circ = 7.5\,\mathrm{Nm}.
  • Along the handle: \sin 0^\circ = 0, no torque at all.

That's what the cross product encodes: \lvert \vec r \times \vec F \rvert = rF\sin\theta.

Work / energy

  • Work is the energy transferred from an object by applying a force along a displacement.
  • Unit: 1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{Ws} → 1\,\mathrm{kWh}? 1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 3.6 \cdot 10^6\,\mathrm{J}.
  • Work is a scalar. It has a magnitude but not a direction.
  • Energy is "stored" work:
E_{pot} = mgh, \qquad E_{th} = cm\Delta T, \qquad E_{kin,L} = m\frac{v^2}{2}, \qquad E_{kin,R} = I\frac{\omega^2}{2}, \qquad E_{el} = UQ = UIt
Symbols
  • E_{pot} — potential energy: m mass (kg), g gravitational acceleration (m/s²), h height (m)
  • E_{th} — thermal energy (heat): c specific heat capacity (J/(kg·K)), \Delta T temperature change (K)
  • E_{kin,L} — linear kinetic energy: v speed (m/s)
  • E_{kin,R} — rotational kinetic energy: I moment of inertia (kg·m²), \omega angular velocity (rad/s)
  • E_{el} — electrical energy: U voltage (V), Q charge (C), I current (A), t time (s)

(potential, heat, kinetic — linear and rotational — and electrical energy)

Power

  • Worker A digs a hole in 2 hours, worker B takes just 1 hour. Both do the same work, but take different times → power.
  • Power = work (energy) / time. Unit: 1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{Nm/s} = 1\,\mathrm{J/s}.
  • A device with 1 kW power running for 1 hour will consume 1 kWh.
P = \frac{E}{t} = Fv = M\omega = UI\cos(\varphi)
Symbols
  • P — power (W); E — energy/work (J); t — time (s)
  • F — force (N); v — velocity (m/s)
  • M — torque (N·m); \omega — angular velocity (rad/s)
  • U — voltage (V); I — current (A); \varphi — phase shift between voltage and current (for AC); \cos(\varphi) — the power factor

Linear (force × velocity), rotary (torque × angular speed) and electrical power; \cos(\varphi) = 1 for DC. For AC, electrical power is a bit more complicated: apparent power, reactive/wattless power. Heat? Friction?

Connection

P = M\omega is the rotational twin of P = Fv: torque replaces force, angular velocity replaces velocity. Remember to use \omega in rad/s: \omega = 2\pi \frac{n}{60} for a speed n in rpm (from the rotation formulas in 2 Dynamics).

Efficiency

  • Efficiency (in engineering) describes how much energy (power) is preserved or transmitted in a process with respect to the input energy (power):
\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} < 100\%
Symbols
  • \eta — efficiency (eta), dimensionless or in %
  • P_{out} — useful output power (W); P_{in} — input power (W)
  • How is energy "lost"? → transformed into something "not useful"?
  • Batteries, motors, gearboxes, …

A chart (Statista, March 2023) compares the efficiency of engines in passenger vehicles: electric highest (about 70%), then diesel, hybrid, fuel cell, gasoline and e-fuels.

Why do efficiencies multiply along a drive chain?

Each stage passes on only a fraction of what it receives. If the motor delivers 35% of the fuel's energy to the gearbox, and the gearbox passes on 95% of that, the wheels get 0.95 \cdot 0.35 of the original. So \eta_{total} = \eta_1 \cdot \eta_2 \cdot \dots — and the total is always below the worst stage, never their average or sum.

Friction

  • From the theory of conservation of energy, we know that energy is always preserved.
  • However, we observe a "loss of energy" in moving objects.
  • Types of friction: gliding, rolling, liquid, air (→ atomic friction), …
  • Resulting energy form: heat.
  • Friction is not always a "bad" thing: mechanical brakes, clutches, heating.

Examples

Example: a DC electric motor rotates at n = 600\,\mathrm{rpm} with a torque of M = 7\,\mathrm{Nm}. The motor consumes 5\,\mathrm{A} at 100\,\mathrm{V}. What is the efficiency of the motor?

Solution: 87.96%.

Another example: a drivetrain is made up of a combustion motor with an efficiency of 35%, which is connected with a clutch to a gearbox with a combined efficiency of 95%. What is the total efficiency of the drivetrain?

Solution: 33.25%.

Worked example: the slide's motor efficiency, step by step
  • Mechanical output power, P = M\omega: first convert the speed: \omega = 2\pi \cdot \frac{600}{60}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}} \approx 62.83\,\mathrm{rad/s}. Then P_{out} = 7 \cdot 62.83\,\mathrm{W} \approx 439.8\,\mathrm{W}.
  • Electrical input power, P = UI: P_{in} = 100 \cdot 5\,\mathrm{W} = 500\,\mathrm{W}.
  • Efficiency: \eta = \frac{439.8}{500} \approx 87.96\% ✓.

The drivetrain: \eta = 0.35 \cdot 0.95 = 0.3325 = 33.25\% ✓ (multiply, as above).

Common mistake: rpm in P = M\omega

7\,\mathrm{Nm} \cdot 600 = 4200 "W" would mean an efficiency of 840% — impossible. \omega must be in rad/s: convert rpm with \omega = 2\pi n / 60. An efficiency above 100% is always a sign of a unit error.
